https://www.bbc.co.uk/news/articles/c24m.text: Image source, Anadolu via Getty Images Image caption, The Ashenda festival is eagerly anticipated by girls and young women in northern Ethiopia By Michael Teferi BBC Africa Published 8 hours ago A major cultural and religious festival celebrating women and the Virgin Mary in northern Ethiopia has been cancelled in Mekelle, the main city in the Tigray region, over fears it may be targeted in drone attacks. The focal point of Ashenda festival, which traditionally draws thousands of young women dressed in their finery, was to be a mass gathering at a stadium in Mekelle on Saturday. Tigray is still recovering from a brutal two-year civil war that ended in 2022. There are concerns the conflict might reignite with the regional authorities blaming a recent series of deadly drone strikes on federal armed forces. The government has not responded to a BBC request for comment on the accusations. Is Ethiopia heading back to war in Tigray? Published 26 February The three-day festival of Ashenda takes places as Orthodox Christians commemorate the Virgin Mary. Its name means "the tall green grass" in Tigrinya and has grown into a wider cultural event that celebrates women. It is eagerly anticipated by girls and young women in Tigray and other parts of northern Ethiopia. They dress up, braid their hair in a special way and are free to dance and play together outside, something which is traditionally frowned upon at other times of the year. The latest drone strike hit Mekelle on Thursday, injuring 13 civilians and damaging homes, Tigray's communications affairs bureau said. Regional officials also reported two drone strikes near Dandera, 15km (nine miles) from Mekelle, on 18 August, saying that one person died and another was injured. They also said that a strike in Raya-Alamata district on 10 August left three dead . Announcing the cancellation of Saturday's stadium gathering Dori Asgedom, head of Tigray's culture and tourism bureau, said it would not be going ahead because of "ongoing drone strikes and the threat of war". "The drone attack on innocent citizens in Mekelle city is an act that history will not forgive and should be condemned," he added. Reflecting on Thursday's attack, the Tigray regional administration called for the "international community to break their silence" and condemn what had happened and "take urgent diplomatic action to prevent further escalation". In 2022, the Tigray People's Liberation Front (TPLF) and the federal government signed a deal ending two years of fighting that its estimated left hundreds of thousands dead. But political tensions this year have raised fears the conflict could start again. This comes after the TPLF removed the interim administration set up under the peace deal and reinstated its pre-war council. Both sides accuse each other of failing to implement the deal. https://www.dw.com/en/freigang-banned-ge.text: Skip to content Skip to main menu Skip to more DW sites https://p.dw.com/p/5PwHi Prefer DW on Google Laura Freigang is already well into her 16-month suspension Image: Michael Memmler/Eibner/picture alliance Advertisement Laura Freigang is set to miss next year's women's World Cup in Brazil after being suspended for missing doping tests, the German Football Association (DFB) said in a statement on Thursday. Freigang, who has played 45 matches for Germany and scored 17 goals, will be suspended until October 7, 2027 after reaching a settlement with the DFB, the World Anti-Doping Agency (WADA) and Germany's National Anti-Doping Agency (NADA). The suspension is for the next 16-months as it began retroactively on June 8, 2026, when she was notified by the DFB, and prohibts Freigang from playing for club or country. "It's important to me to emphasize once again that I was never suspected of doping," Freigang said in a statement on Instagram. "My agreement to a settlement does not mean that I share all the assessments of my case. The past few months have been extremely difficult for me. Another legal process would have entailed significant financial, mental, and emotional strain. This is why I decided to take this path, in the hope of finding some peace, clarity and perspective for myself," she added. "It was never my intention to let it get this far. Sports have defined my life since I was little. It breaks my heart that, for now, I won't be able to step onto the field, help my team, or live the daily life that I love so much." End of an ongoing process for Freigang This brings to a close a case that has been ongoing for months. The 28-year-old had been accused of not being where she said she would be for a doping control on three occasions between March 2025 and February 2026. In June of this year, Freigang explained missing the tests "were not deliberately avoided appointments but inconsistencies or misunderstandings in the comprehensive details that have to be updated daily and which we as national team players have to update in the system on a daily and hourly basis." The ban ends her World Cup hopes, something the DFB has also acknowledged. "We are simply so sorry for Laura on a personal level because of this situation. The past few weeks have been very stressful for her," said DFB Sporting Director Nia Künzer. "We hold her in high regard both as a player and as a person, and — as we have done in recent weeks — we will continue to stay in touch with her and support her as best we can." The situation also puts her future at her club, Eintracht Frankfurt, into question. Freigang's contract runs until June next year. "The agreement that has now been reached provides clarity and planning certainty through a process that is unique to Eintracht Frankfurt — for us as a club, but above all for Laura," Katharina Kiel, Frankfurt's director of women's football, said. The club and Freigang, who has played 180 Bundesliga games in her career, are now set to enter talks to determine the shape of her contract moving forward.
